```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
include("_setup.jl")
using CovarianceMatrices: EWC
using LinearAlgebra: diag
```

Mikkel Plagborg-Møller's short course *Local projections for applied
macroeconomics* (2026) works one example through its Stata code: the effect of
global temperature shocks on world GDP, after Bilal and Känzig (2026). This page
reruns two of its steps that the package did not have: the **variance
decomposition** of lecture 1, which asks how much of the GDP forecast error the
temperature shock explains, and the **joint inference** of lecture 3, a Wald test
of all horizons at once and a simultaneous confidence band. In Stata they take a
loop of `regress`/`predict`, `suest` and a user-written command; here they are
`implicitfevd`, `jointtest` and `bands = :supt`.

## Data and specification

The course's extract of the Bilal–Känzig data ships as
`docs/src/data/bilal_kanzig.csv`: annual, 1960–2019, with world real GDP per
capita (100·log, `lnrgdppc_world_pwt`), the global temperature anomaly
(`gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s`, the Hamilton-filter forecast error of global temperature
in °C), a global-recession indicator, the log oil price and the one-year Treasury
yield.

```{julia}
bk = bk_data()
first(bk[:, [:year, :lnrgdppc_world_pwt, :gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s, :recessiondates]], 3)
```

With $y_t$ log GDP, $x_t$ the anomaly, $r_t$ the recession indicator and $w_t$ the
four lagged series, the local projection is

$$
y_{t+h} = \mu_h + \theta_h x_t + \sum_{j=0}^{2} \gamma_{h,j} r_{t-j}
        + \sum_{j=1}^{2} \delta_{h,j}' w_{t-j} + \xi_{h,t+h}, \qquad h = 0, \dots, 10,
$$

with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors, the course's
`reg ..., robust`. This is the argument of Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller
(2021): once the projection controls for lags of the data (lag augmentation), the
conventional heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are valid, with no HAC
correction and no bandwidth to choose. A recent version of the LP–VAR primer of
Montiel Olea, Plagborg-Møller, Qian and Wolf (2025) goes one step further:

> The LP estimator should be bias-corrected using the procedure of Herbst and
> Johannsen (2024). Instead of reporting HAC standard errors for LP, simply report
> the conventional heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors—or even better, the
> bootstrap confidence interval discussed in Supplemental Appendix B.

The package has both: `biascorrect(m)` for the Herbst–Johannsen correction and
`varbootstrap(m, data; vars, nlags)` for that bootstrap. This page stays with the
course's HC1 standard errors.

```{julia}
m = lp(@formula(leads(lnrgdppc_world_pwt) ~ gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s + recessiondates +
                lags(recessiondates, 2) + lags(lnrgdppc_world_pwt, 2) +
                lags(gtmp_bkly_aw_dtfe2s, 2) + lags(lnpoil_wti, 2) + lags(treasury1y, 2)),
       bk; horizon = 10)
summarize(m; level = 0.68)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
θ = coefpath(m)
x̃ = implicitshock(m)
sdx = std(filter(isfinite, x̃))
```

A 1 °C anomaly lowers world GDP per capita by `{julia} f2(-θ[5])`% after four years
and `{julia} f2(-θ[7])`% after six.

## The implicit shock

By Frisch–Waugh, $\theta_h$ is the response to $\tilde x_t$, the residual of $x_t$
on all the controls: the movement in temperature that recessions and past
economic conditions do not explain. `implicitshock` returns it, aligned with the
rows of the data:

```{julia}
x̃ = implicitshock(m)
std(filter(isfinite, x̃))
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The implicit temperature shock (°C), the residual of the anomaly on the controls."
#| fig-height: 2.6
ok = isfinite.(x̃)
p = plot(bk.year[ok], x̃[ok]; c = INK, lw = 1.4, base()..., title = "implicit shock, °C")
hline!(p, [0.0]; c = RULE, ls = :dot, lw = 0.8)
plot(p; size = (720, 260), FIGKW...)
```

Its standard deviation, `{julia} f2(sdx)` °C, is the size of a typical shock, so
a 1 °C impulse is about `{julia} round(Int, 1 / sdx)` standard deviations, an
unusually large one.

## Variance decomposition

How much of the uncertainty about future GDP is due to temperature shocks? The
course's recipe, a version of Gorodnichenko and Lee (2020), runs at each horizon
two regressions:

1. regress $y_{t+h}$ on the controls (everything but $x_t$) and keep the forecast
   error $\hat f_{h,t+h}$;
2. regress $\hat f_{h,t+h}$ on a constant and $\tilde x_t, \tilde x_{t+1}, \dots,
   \tilde x_{t+h}$; the share is its $R^2$.

The share is the fraction of the forecast-error variance that would disappear if
the current and future shocks were known. `implicitfevd` runs both steps from the
fitted projection:

```{julia}
fv = implicitfevd(m)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Share of the forecast-error variance of world GDP due to temperature shocks."
#| fig-height: 2.8
p = plot(0:10, fv.share; c = INK, lw = 1.8, marker = :circle, ms = 3, msw = 0,
         mc = INK, ylims = (0, 0.6), xticks = 0:10, base()...,
         title = "share of forecast-error variance", xlabel = "horizon (years)")
plot(p; size = (720, 280), FIGKW...)
```

Temperature shocks explain `{julia} round(100 * fv.share[3]; digits = 1)`% of the
variance of the two-year GDP forecast error and
`{julia} round(100 * fv.share[8]; digits = 1)`% of the seven-year one, the figures
on the course's slides.

The package's `fevd`, the port of Gorodnichenko and Lee's own code, would not
accept this specification as it stands: it treats the shock as observed and
demeaned rather than residualized, conditions only on lagged variables, and needs
a `cumul` or `ldiff` response. `implicitfevd` follows the course instead: the shock
is $\tilde x_t$, the forecast error conditions on the contemporaneous recession
indicator too, and the $R^2$ is the centred one of a regression with a constant.
It has no standard errors, as in the course.

## Joint inference across horizons

The 68% band above covers each horizon with probability 0.68 *separately*. A
hypothesis about several horizons needs the covariance of the estimates across
horizons, which are correlated because the regressions share their observations.
`jointvcov` stacks the scores of every horizon on one time axis (Stata's `suest`),
and `jointtest` is the Wald test that the response is zero at every horizon:

```{julia}
t = jointtest(m)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
V = jointvcov(m)
R = V ./ sqrt.(diag(V) * diag(V)')
```

The estimates are strongly correlated across neighbouring horizons (the
correlation of $\hat\theta_5$ and $\hat\theta_6$ is `{julia} f2(R[6, 7])`), so the
pointwise band cannot be read as a joint statement. The null of no effect at any
horizon is rejected with a p-value of `{julia} f3(t.pvalue)`.

A **simultaneous** band covers the whole response with probability 0.68. The
sup-t band of Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2019) widens the pointwise band by
a common critical value, the 68% quantile of $\max_h |\hat\theta_h - \theta_h| /
\mathrm{se}_h$, simulated from that correlation:

```{julia}
c68 = supt_critical_value(m; level = 0.68)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Response of world GDP per capita (%) to a 1 °C temperature shock: 68% pointwise band (shaded) and 68% sup-t simultaneous band (dashed)."
#| fig-height: 3.2
s_pw = summarize(m; level = 0.68)
s_si = summarize(m; level = 0.68, bands = :supt)
p = plot(0:10, s_pw.lower; fillrange = s_pw.upper, linealpha = 0, fillcolor = INK,
         fillalpha = BANDALPHA, xticks = 0:10, base()...,
         title = "response of world GDP (%) to a 1 °C shock", xlabel = "horizon (years)")
plot!(p, 0:10, [s_si.lower s_si.upper]; c = ACCENT, ls = :dash, lw = 1.2)
hline!(p, [0.0]; c = RULE, ls = :dot, lw = 0.8)
plot!(p, 0:10, s_pw.coef; c = INK, lw = 1.8, marker = :circle, ms = 3, msw = 0, mc = INK)
plot(p; size = (720, 320), FIGKW...)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
excl(s) = findall((s.upper .< 0) .| (s.lower .> 0)) .- 1
s90 = summarize(m; level = 0.90, bands = :supt)
hrange(v) = length(v) > 1 && v == collect(first(v):last(v)) ? "$(first(v))–$(last(v))" : join(v, ", ")
```

The simultaneous band uses `{julia} f2(c68)` standard errors instead of one. It
still excludes zero at horizons `{julia} hrange(excl(s_si))`, so the negative effect
of temperature shocks on GDP survives the joint reading. At the 90% level
(critical value `{julia} f2(supt_critical_value(m; level = 0.9))`) it excludes zero
at horizons `{julia} hrange(excl(s90))`. Any shape restriction can be checked the
same way: a monotone response, for instance, is rejected if no monotone function
fits inside the band.

`bands = :supt` works in `summarize`, `plot` and `irfplot` alike:

```julia
summarize(m; level = 0.68, bands = :supt)
plot(m; levels = [0.68], bands = :supt)
```

With an `EWC(B)` estimator the test becomes the fixed-smoothing $F_{m,\,B-m+1}$
test and the sup-t draws come from the fixed-$b$ limit, whose margins are
Student-$t_B$. With $T = 58$ the LLSW rule gives only
`{julia} ewc_bandwidth(m)` cosine terms, fewer than the eleven horizons, and an
EWC variance has rank at most $B$, so the joint test is available only for a few
horizons at a time:

```{julia}
jointtest(m, EWC(ewc_bandwidth(m)); horizons = 4:8)
```
